extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology/psychoanalysis, literary theorists, and researchers of humour and jokes
extracted.subtask_description: Psychoanalytic and aesthetic account of what a joke is, how jokes differ from the comic and humour, and the verbal/psychic techniques by which jokes produce their effect. Focuses on formal features (wording, condensation, substitution) and psychical mechanisms (unconscious/preconscious interplay, economies of expenditure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity (conciseness) as essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity is 'the body and the soul of wit'; a joke often says what it has to say in too few words and may even say it by not saying it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes commonly compress or omit explanatory material; the comic effect often depends on preserving that compression. Example: Heine's 'famillionär' replaces an explanatory clause and thereby creates the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bringing forward what is hidden
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke must 'bring forward something that is concealed or hidden' (akin to caricature uncovering concealed ugliness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes frequently reveal or allude to suppressed, concealed, or subsidiary thoughts; effective jokes make implicit content accessible by form or phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful judgement / activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are characterized as a 'playful judgement'—an active, subject-centered operation rather than a passive object-like perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion emphasizes the joker's active stance: jokes are produced by a subjective, playful appraisal rather than merely observed phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupling dissimilar things / binding alien ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Joking often consists in rapid binding together of ideas that are in fact alien to one another (finding hidden similarities or surprising unities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many jokes hinge on unexpected juxtapositions or unities of otherwise unrelated concepts; useful technique is to link two disparate domains to produce surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast / sense in nonsense
rubrics_metrics.description: A common determinant is a contrast between ideas (or between meaning and meaninglessness)—we momentarily grant significance and then deny it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes can operate by attributing, then withdrawing, sense; examples include remarks that seem to have logical consequences which are immediately undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bewilderment followed by illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic effect can derive from initial bewilderment (confusion) resolved by sudden understanding—the two-stage process of 'bewilderment and illumination'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective jokes often first puzzle the listener (a nonce word, strange phrasing), then provide an immediate reinterpretation that dissolves the puzzle (e.g., 'famillionär').

rubrics_metrics.name: Form/wording determines jokehood
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an utterance is funny often depends on its verbal expression rather than on the underlying thought; the same thought expressed plainly may not be a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or crafting jokes, attend to precise phrasing: shifts in wording, compression, or morphological play can turn an ordinary observation into a laugh-provoking joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation as basic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke formation frequently involves a process analogous to Freudian condensation: multiple elements are compressed, with some parts suppressed and others fused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for how two sentences or ideas are collapsed into one expression that preserves suggestive components of the omitted material (e.g., merging 'familiär' + 'Millionär').

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of substitutes / composite words
rubrics_metrics.description: A substitute (often a composite word) is formed to stand for suppressed material; composite words fuse overlapping syllables from two words to suggest omitted content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'famillionär' (familiär + Millionär), 'anecdotage' (anecdote + dotage); composite forms economize expression while pointing to omitted clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation accompanied by slight modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes condensation is realized by a small change (a single letter/phoneme) that substitutes for the omitted material and evokes it indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, nearly imperceptible textual changes (mispronunciations, letter swaps) can suggest the suppressed idea—examples include transforming 'tête-à-tête' to imply 'ass' by changing 't' to 'b'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution by representation (opposite/absurd)
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitute for suppressed content may take the form of a representation by the opposite or by something absurd, thereby hinting at the omitted thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'a great future behind him' replaces the expected 'before' to imply that the subject's prospects are reversed; substitutes may operate by irony or inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wordplay, puns and apparent misprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Punning, playful morphological manipulation, and 'misprint'-like constructions are standard technical methods for producing jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include blending words, punning on similar forms, exploiting polysemy, or presenting an apparent typographical error that yields a humorous reinterpretation (e.g., 'Orienterpresszug').

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation with interpenetration (fusion without neat composite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes constituents interpenetrate rather than forming a neat composite word; elements of two sources blend more diffusely to form the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'roter Fadian' fuses 'roter Faden' with a pejorative sense—assessing such jokes requires tracing both source components and their associative links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slighter modification tends to improve effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the slighter the modification (the closer the substitute to ordinary expression), the more effective the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimal departures from standard phrasing that nevertheless evoke omitted meaning often produce stronger humorous effects than clumsy or large alterations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke as compromise between unconscious and preconscious
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychically, jokes are formed as a compromise between unconscious material and preconscious expression—one interpretive track invokes unconscious associations while the other is conscious wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand jokes as structurally mediating suppressed content: effective jokes allow unconscious associations to surface masked by surface expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Janus-head / dual ideational processing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure from a joke arises from simultaneously applying two different ideational methods to the same content—one passing through the unconscious and one remaining at the surface—producing a 'double face'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing jokes, identify the two readings (surface/readily conscious and the deeper/unconscious inference) and how their mismatch generates pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of inhibition / psychic expenditure (source of pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of jokes derives from an economy in expenditure upon inhibition—savings in the psychic work required to suppress forbidden content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a joke permits release of suppressed affect/idea with relatively little inhibitory cost; this economy explains why certain disguised expressions are pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among joke, comic, and humour localization
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is localized in preconscious ideational processes, humour is closer to preconscious affective displacement, while jokes involve a compromise between unconscious and preconscious processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to classify instances: if the effect depends on pure contrast/expectation at the conscious/preconscious level, label it 'comic'; if it displaces emotions (pity, anger) into pleasure, label 'humour'; if it evokes suppressed associations via wording, label 'joke'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and function classification (technique vs. rhetorical use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes can be classified both by technical method (pun, condensation, caricature) and by use in speech (caricature, characterization, snubs, social functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or composing jokes, note both the structural technique employed and the pragmatic function the joke serves in discourse (e.g., satire, ridicule, social bonding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of feeling as mechanism of humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour (distinct from jokes) operates by economizing feeling—avoiding or reducing an affect (pity, anger, disgust) and converting it into pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify cases where humour works by thwarting an expected emotional response (e.g., a stoic remark in face of tragedy) and thus produces laughter through inhibited affect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition and anti-expectation as humorous devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (monotony) and subversion of expected reactions (e.g., the subject's nonchalance where anger/pity was expected) produce humour by thwarting anticipated affective responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that repeatedly neutralize or invert expected outcomes (e.g., Mark Twain's anecdotes) produce humour by defusing prepared emotions into laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise by reattribution of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke often surprises by reattributing or reinterpreting the meaning of a word/phrase so that initial sense is undermined and a new, comic sense replaces it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for mechanisms where semantic reinterpretation (literalizing a metaphor, fusing words) flips the listener's understanding, producing comic illumination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of material to oral tradition and social circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes often survive and spread because they are apt for oral transmission and social currency; popularity can be an indicator of a joke's effective compression and resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a joke's success, consider how readily it can be reproduced, its economy of wording, and its capacity to evoke shared knowledge or associations.
